transcript.text: Good morning
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Hi, this is Michelin Meyer.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I’m renting your house on Archwood Avenue.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I’m due to move in next week.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Oh, yes.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Hello, Ms.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Meyer.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: What can I do for you?
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: When I viewed the house, I told you I’ll most probably need to rent some furniture, at least until I know whether my temporary work contract is going to be made permanent.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Yes, of course.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: I remember.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: And I said I could give you some information about furniture rental companies in the city.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: That’s right.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Well, the biggest company is called Peak Rentals.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: I’ve recommended them to other people and have always heard positive reports about them.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Could you give me an idea of their costs?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Sure.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: I actually have one of their brochures here.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: It says the monthly price per room starts at $105 and goes up to $239.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: That depends on which rooms you need furniture for, of course.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Sure.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: It’s just to get a general idea of how much it’s going to cost.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: And you said you had some positive feedback about this company?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: People have mentioned that the furniture from Peak Rentals is more modern than any of the other companies.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: And also, once you place an order, the furniture will be delivered to you in just one or two days.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: That would be really helpful.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Oh, and the brochure says that there’s a special offer at the moment.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: If you rent living room furniture, I believe that’s a set of chairs and a TV table, you’ll also get a lamp at no extra cost.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Okay, but you know, that price range you gave is more than I was hoping to pay.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Then you could try Aaron and Oliver.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Sorry, what and Oliver?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Aaron, double A-R-O-N
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: OK, are they cheaper
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I'd say they are a mid-range company.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: But if you chose them you need to be aware that they charge an extra 12% every month in case of damage
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Oh, I see.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I’d have to do the math carefully then.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: But one helpful thing is that they also do cleaning for customers.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: For the furniture?
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: For the house.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Oh, I see.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I probably won’t need that.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: There’s another company called Larch Furniture.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: It’s quite new, and it has the lowest prices in town.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: That’s for both furniture and also electronic equipment.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Well, that would be good.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I’m not bringing much with me, and I won’t have much time to go shopping after I start my job.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: There are two things you need to know about Larch Furniture.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: First of all you have to take out insurance on the furniture and you need to organize that yourself
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: That wouldn’t be too hard.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Also you can't take out a contract for less than six months but I figure that might not be a problem for you.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: You’re renting the house for 12 months after all, aren’t you?
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Yes, okay.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Well, I…
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Sorry to interrupt.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: I just thought of another furniture rental company.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: It’s called Space Rentals, and it’s located very near to the house.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Okay.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I don’t have any information about their charges, so it’s best to use their app to find out what it would cost you to use them.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: Okay, thanks.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: I’ll do that.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: One good thing about that company is that if you don’t like the furniture once it’s delivered, you can request exchanges, as long as you do that within a week of receiving it.
transcript.speaker: MAN

transcript.text: That sounds really great.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: Okay, well, thanks very much.
transcript.speaker: WOMAN

transcript.text: That’s so helpful

transcript.text: Hello, I’m Hayden.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: I’m one of the archaeologists investigating the site here at Bidcuster.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: This is the third summer for this community project, and most of the people digging here are volunteers.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: I’m a full-time archaeologist for the town council, but I was asked to join the project by NHA, a charity which sets up projects like this up and down the country.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: As you can see, we’re next to Bidcaster Castle, which is great because the owners let us use their facilities.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: So, how did we get to where we are today?
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: Many archaeology projects happen when an ancient object is found, and in our case that object was a gold coin.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: Coins are often found by people using metal detectors to look for things buried in the ground or coins are uncovered when wild animals like rabbits have been digging tunnels.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: Here, a walker found it on the ground after a rainstorm washed away some of the earth and sand.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: When the story of the gold coin hit the news, Peter Swift, an amateur historian, contacted me to say he believed there had been a village on this site, centuries before the castle was built.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: Just by chance, the team found some old maps and documents in our library, which showed 500-year-old drawings of ruined buildings on the grassy area between the outer stone walls of the castle and the river.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: We knew then we were onto something.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: Over the three summers the team has been here, we’ve found the remains of several buildings, and more broken pots than you can count.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: Normally you’d expect to find brooches and other jewellery, but we’re still waiting to uncover any such items.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: The people who once lived here were skilled at making tools from animal bones, as you’ll see when you visit the exhibition.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: Besides the discovery of the village, we’ve also found evidence of human activity on the other side of the river.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: No other houses or huts so far, but we can see the borders of an ancient field system.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: At one point we found a long wall and thought it was an ancient palace, but it turned out to be a modern wall.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: This summer’s work will end soon, but we’ll be back next summer.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: In the meantime, we’re putting on a series of guided tours for school groups this autumn.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: Oh, and maybe you saw the TV documentary about our project.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: That suggests the objects we’ve found are going to the town’s museum, but we don’t know that for sure yet.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: When you enter the site, please make sure you keep to the paths at all times.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: There are a few other things, the highlights of the site if you like, that I want to mention.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: Take a look at the map.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: Our present location is marked at the bottom.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: This year, we’ve identified the foundations of an ancient bridge, and it’s really exciting today because a team of divers are in the river searching for lost objects.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: To reach the bridge, take the main path ahead of you, go straight on, and keep going till the path bends to the left.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: You’ll see a smaller track leading off to the right.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: Follow that to take you to the river, where the divers are.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: You might be interested to see the rubbish pit.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: This is very near the castle walls in the north-west corner of the site.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: It actually dates to the time of the castle and not the ancient village.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: We found oyster shells and fish bones, and we assumed they were thrown from the castle kitchen above.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: One area we excavated in the first summer uncovered the site of a meeting hall.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: We knew it was an important building because it had two rows of post holes, deep enough to support a large roof.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: It is the largest structure in the central area of the site next to the current excavation area.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: Last year we discovered a fish pond in the ancient village.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: Normally these were beside a river.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: The pond here is further away, but it’s possible the river has moved slightly.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: Anyway, to get there from here, you turn right at the first information board you come to and follow the path into the trees.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: Before you come out of the trees, you’ll see it on your right.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: If you reach the river, you’ve gone too far.
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: So, does anyone have…
transcript.speaker: HAYDEN

transcript.text: So, Finn, I’ve done as much as I can for our project on theatre programmes.
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: How’s your research coming along?
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: OK, Maya.
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: I didn’t know theatre programmes are called playbills in the USA till I started looking into the topic.
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: Even though I struggled to find many useful websites, I’m glad we picked this subject.
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: No one else on the course is doing the same as us, although it is one of the research areas of the module convener.
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: That might actually put some people off.
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: I suppose so.
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: Anyway I hadn’t realised there are actually companies specialising in creating theatre programmes
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: Yes they are quite common nowadays.
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: Contrary to what many people think, theatres don’t hire people to do the programmes.
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: In fact, companies buy the rights to publish programmes on the theatre’s behalf and then make their money selling advertising space within the programme booklet.
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: It must be easier for theatres to do it that way.
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: I remember reading something about programmes in early British theatre.
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: It said that the cast was always very important.
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: Yeah, audiences were very familiar with leading actors and big names would draw huge crowds.
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: But I hadn’t realised that if the programme named a famous actor, that’s who the public expected to perform.
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: And if that didn’t happen, people accused the theatre of breaking their agreement with the audience.
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: They would demand refunds and if they didn’t get them, there were riots.
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: Outrageous!
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: That’d never happen now.
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: No, people are too polite, even when they’re disappointed if the star of the show misses a performance.
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: We should definitely include that information about early audiences in our project.
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: I also think it’s important to mention that lots of ordinary people at that time were illiterate, so theatre programmes were of limited value in advertising plays.
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: When a company of actors arrived in a town, they’d parade around the streets in their costumes, beating drums and announcing their upcoming performances.
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: Interesting.
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: I couldn’t imagine that happening now either.
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: There’s also an interesting comparison to make between 18th and 19th century programmes.
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: Wasn’t it in the 19th century that theatre programmes started to resemble programs today
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: Yes and unlike programs from the 18th century they always used colour
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: And there was a greater variety of designs.
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: But personally I think 18th century programmes were superior because they told the theatregoers so many things, including about the actors.
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: And about the writer, the plot and sometimes the history of the play.
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: That’s right.
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: What should we say about theatre programmes in the 20th century?
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: I reckon the most important thing is the dramatic change they underwent during World War II.
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: When the government imposed restrictions on the use of paper.
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: Yeah, but that was only in the UK.
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: In the USA, programmes, or rather playbills, continued to be published in the same format.
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: While here in the UK, programmes became merely a single sheet of paper folded to create four pages for text.
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: What I don’t really get is that after the war they didn’t go back to being more than one sheet or change in any way for over 25 years.
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: I know there were paper shortages after the war, but only for five or ten years.
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: Strange.
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: I got some pictures of programmes we could include on the slides for our presentation.
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: I found a couple too Maya.
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: Let's go through and see what we think
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: Um oh this is an old one for a play called Ruy Blas
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: Never heard of that.
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: But the programme looks very decorative.
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: Good enough to put in a frame on the wall.
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: The images are just beautiful.
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: Finn, what did you find?
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: I’ve got some pages from a programme for Man of La Mancha.
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: I thought this was a good programme to show, not because of the pictures, but because it contains articles written by members of the theatre company, so we can learn how the production was created and the thoughts and feelings of the cast.
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: Good.
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: I’ve got a copy of a programme that’s now in a museum.
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: It’s for The Tragedy of Jane Shore and it’s said to be the earliest surviving document to have been printed on Australia’s first printing press
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: Fantastic!
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: Another programme to talk about is for The Sailors Festival.
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: It comes from the British Library’s digitised collection of programmes that was started a few years ago.
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: It already comprises over 200,000 programmes which is amazing!
transcript.speaker: MAYA

transcript.text: Huh.
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: Wish I’d known about it while I was doing my research.
transcript.speaker: FINN

transcript.text: It’s only relatively recently that designers have become aware of the need to be inclusive when designing products.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But what does that mean exactly?
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Well, it simply means designing products that span economic, social and cultural barriers.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: It means making sure products are accessible, so that as many different types of people as possible can use them, without any type of adaptation having to be made to the original design.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Inclusive design is often linked with universal design, although they are not quite the same thing.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Universal design aims to make products that work for everyone and that includes considering the needs of people who have cognitive difficulties, which can present quite a challenge.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Today examples of successful inclusive design can be seen all around us.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: In workplaces it is common to see desks which can be adjusted to suit people of different heights or for wheelchair users This still isn’t always the case, however, and is one reason why office workers often suffer from back or neck problems.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: You’ll find another example in the public toilets of countless hotels, airports and offices.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Taps that you activate by sensor require no pressing or twisting movements.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: These are not only more hygienic, they’re also easier for people with dexterity or mobility issues.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The tech industry has been criticised in the past for focusing too much on young consumers, but this is changing.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Many products are now designed with the elderly in mind.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: For example, it’s well known that vision declines with age and that we also become worse at distinguishing between similar colours, in particular shades of blue, which is why software designers rarely create interfaces with this colour.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Motor skills also decline with age and some people have difficulty doing everyday things like picking up a cup or opening a door.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This can also affect their ability to use a mouse or keyboard.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: So voice access is now a routine way of making commands.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: It’s worth looking at the problems non-inclusive designs cause when not enough consideration is given to a range of users, as it can have a serious impact on people’s lives.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Access is one obvious example because it has such a huge impact on disabled people’s independence.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Not being able to access public transport because buses or trains are not wheelchair means many disabled people can go out unless someone goes with them.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Safety is another issue.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Inexplicably, most cars are still crash-tested using a dummy based on an average-sized male.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This has safety implications for all women, particularly those who are pregnant, as the seatbelts worn by the dummy are not adapted to accommodate them.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Over the past 100 years, workplaces in the UK have, on the whole, become considerably safer.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Employers are legally required to provide well-maintained personal protective equipment, or PPE, anything from goggles to full bodysuits, to workers who need it, free of charge.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But most PPE is designed to fit men.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: A recent report found that employers often think that when it comes to female workers, all they need to do to comply with this legal requirement is to buy jackets, for example, designed for a small man.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The problem with this is that women can be tall and still have much smaller shoulders than the average man.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Ill-fitting PPE such as high-vis jackets, vests and body armour can put women at risk.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The report found that 95% of women said that their PPE often hampered their work and that this problem was worst in the emergency services, particularly the police.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Another problem is related to comfort at work.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: A very common scenario in offices in summertime is to see women wrapped in blankets or wearing sweaters while the air conditioning is on high.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Meanwhile, the men are in shorts and T-shirts.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This is due to differences in metabolic rates for men and women.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: There is a standard setting for air conditioning to be at a temperature of 21 degrees designed to suit men and in most modern offices it is not possible to turn the air conditioning up or down.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This means that many offices which mainly employ women are wasting energy by having the air conditioning set too high.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: As you can see from the examples I’ve just mentioned, there are serious consequences for designs which don’t consider the needs of all users.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER
